rv.q: Luckily for us it just opened on Broadway, after a recent run Off — and it’s the rare transfer where the show improved.
And now, with a cast including Sigourney Weaver and David Hyde Pierce, he has one of the funniest comedies that Broadway has seen in seasons.
Christopher Durang's riff on Chekhov is an inspired comedy that manages to be both reverent toward and gently mocking of the Russian master's themes.
All of that makes this flawed play disproportionately pleasurable in Nicholas Martin's vibrant, perfectly cast production.

I can think of no more deliriously funny moment from this theater season than what transpires when Ms. Nielsen, playing Sonia, a middle-aged, morbidly depressed woman, swans onstage in a sequined evening gown, with a tiara shimmering on her head and a new glitter of self-confidence in her eyes.

The combination of Durang's witty, incisive writing and Posner's enlightened direction makes this production a farce with a point, a piercing comedy about the serious subject of how well and badly family members treat one another.
Like its Chekhovian characters, Vanya and Sonia and Masha and Spike is assembled from mismatched parts and is desperate for affection, which it miraculously earns.
Both breathtakingly funny and quietly poignant, this Chekhov-inspired work—for which knowledge of the Russian master’s plays is not a requirement—is pure joy from start to finish.
The play is filled with inside theater jokes, scorching barbs, and real soul.
Don't be deceived by the dazzling zaniness of Vanya and Sonia and Masha and Spike. In Christopher Durang's hugely entertaining new play, there's a perilously fine line between comedy and tragedy.
Like the play's lonely, bitter characters, I'm so happy that I can stop complaining.
Whatever he borrows from long-dead Russian playwrights, Vanya and Sonia... is entirely, indisputably, oh-no-he-didn't classic Durang.
That aside, this is a smart, relentlessly silly, at times heartwarming comedy.
A classy show in every way, this admirable play and its fine production are certain to be contenders for all sorts of awards at the end of the current Broadway season.

cn.t: Durang's Chekhov-inspired comedy delights critics as Broadway's funniest offering in seasons, blending sharp wit with poignant melancholy. The stellar cast, led by Weaver and Pierce, delivers razor-sharp performances in this wildly entertaining crowd-pleaser.
